extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys and agents) drafting and litigating patents, especially on §101/Alice issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent specifications and claims and for supporting pleadings so claims survive 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo) challenges; includes what to include in complaints, declarations, and claim drafting to show inventive concept or technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide 'problem/solution' in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting your patent application, consider providing 'problem/solution' in the specification to highlight the various inventive concepts of your software related invention as an improvement over known prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly stating advantages of your inventive concept may help support the inventive concept captured in your claims as not routine or conventional (example: Aatrix’s claimed 'data file contains an inventive concept directed to improved importation of data and interoperability with third-party software').

rubrics_metrics.name: Support asserted claims in pleadings with specification evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing a complaint, consider providing support from your patent specification that your asserted claims include inventive concepts that are not routine and conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include citations and excerpts from the specification and any declarations that tie claimed limitations to described inventive concepts to avoid early dismissal under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factual allegations/evidence to oppose §101 dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausible factual allegations may preclude dismissing a case under §101 where 'nothing on th[e] record...refutes those allegations as a matter of law or justifies dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6).' (Aatrix)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit declarations or factual pleadings that, taken as true, would directly affect the court’s Alice patent-eligibility analysis (e.g., evidence that claimed elements are unconventional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts must state reasoning/evidence before deeming components 'well understood' or 'routine'
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court should provide reasoning or evidence when finding that a claimed component 'describes a well understood and routine component and function of a computer' rather than asserting that conclusion without support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and rebut blanket characterizations of claim elements as 'routine' by documenting why elements are unconventional or how they operate differently from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific in the specification about how the invention operates to provide an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting specifications, consider being specific with respect to how the invention operates to provide an improvement over the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the concrete technical benefits, the mechanism by which the benefits are achieved, and how the claimed arrangement departs from earlier approaches (examples: distributed enhancement for data flows, storing verification structure in BIOS memory, parser transforming data to improve functionality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe interactions and operations of (possibly conventional) components that act in an unconventional manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider carefully describing interactions and operations between components that may be considered conventional to relate a story of how these components act in an unconventional manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how generic components operate together in a non-conventional way to achieve a technological improvement (e.g., specific ordering or configuration that produces improved computer functionality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim specific ways/means of achieving results (not only results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully review the claims to determine if the claims are directed to the result rather than how to solve the problem at hand; the distinction between results and means is fundamental to eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to recite how the desired result is achieved (concrete steps, structures, configuration), not merely the desired outcome; ensure claimed features that effect the solution are actually claimed, not only described in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leaving implementation to unbounded trial-and-error
rubrics_metrics.description: A direction to engage in a conventional, unbounded trial-and-error process (e.g., perform a plurality of experiments) does not make a patent-eligible invention, even if the desired result would be new and unconventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific guidance, parameters, tuning instructions, or concrete techniques in the specification and claims rather than instructions that require open-ended experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sufficient detail in application and claims (extend detail to dependent claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient detail should be included in the application draft describing the solution to the problem rather than simply applying a natural law or mathematical formula; this should be extended to the claim scope where, at the very least, dependent claims should include limitations with sufficient detail to describe the solution to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dependent claims to narrow and define how the invention achieves its effects and to preserve claim scope that may bear on eligibility and enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims may affect §101 — do not concede one claim is representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims can bear on patent eligibility; plaintiffs should not concede that a single representative independent claim covers all claims for §101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and preserve arguments based on dependent-claim limitations that may supply an inventive concept or technical improvement; analyze multiple claims rather than relying on a single representative claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether elements are 'well-understood, routine and conventional' is a question of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing Alice step two, the question of whether a claim element or combination of elements is well-understood, routine and conventional to a skilled artisan in the relevant field is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build factual record (expert declarations, technical evidence, specification support) to create genuine issues of material fact where appropriate; absent factual disputes, courts may decide the issue as a matter of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show inventive concept in ordered combination or unconventional arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept can be found in the non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known, conventional pieces; claims may be eligible because they recite a specific discrete implementation that provides a technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims that carve out a specific implementation (location, arrangement, customization) and explain how that arrangement improves computer functionality or solves a technical problem (e.g., remote ISP server with per-user filtering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid describing elements as 'conventional' or relying on well-known business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your specification contains details of how claimed functionality is performed and avoids characterization of elements that are claimed as conventional or typical or commonly known; also avoid referencing well-known business practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is a technical problem, describe specifics of how the technical problem is solved rather than labeling components as generic or invoking business-practice rationales that the court may treat as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide implementation details when dependent claims must demonstrate inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should provide details of how claimed functions are implemented, especially if dependent claims are relied on to show inventive concept; for at least some dependent claims the specification should describe how to implement claimed functions (e.g., linking an order to a table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the specification contains examples, flow, structures, or algorithms that concretely implement claimed functions to avoid claims being treated as merely aspirational or result-oriented.
